scienceFacts.title: Octopuses have three hearts
scienceFacts.description: Two pump blood to the gills, while the third circulates it to the rest of the body. The main heart stops beating when they swim, which is why they prefer crawling.

scienceFacts.title: Bananas are radioactive
scienceFacts.description: Bananas contain potassium-40, a naturally radioactive isotope. The dose is tiny and harmless, but real enough that shipments of bananas can trigger radiation sensors at ports.

scienceFacts.title: Honey never spoils
scienceFacts.description: Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs, over 3,000 years old, still perfectly edible. Its low moisture and acidic pH prevent microbes from growing.

scienceFacts.title: A day on Venus is longer than its year
scienceFacts.description: Venus rotates so slowly that a single day (243 Earth days) is longer than the time it takes to orbit the Sun (225 Earth days).

scienceFacts.title: Humans share 60% of their DNA with bananas
scienceFacts.description: Most of that shared DNA controls basic cellular functions common to all life on Earth, like metabolism and cell division.

scienceFacts.title: Sharks predate trees
scienceFacts.description: Sharks have been swimming Earth's oceans for around 400 million years, roughly 50 million years longer than trees have existed on land.

scienceFacts.title: Water can boil and freeze at the same time
scienceFacts.description: At the triple point of water (0.01 C and low pressure), water exists simultaneously as a solid, liquid, and gas.

scienceFacts.title: The Eiffel Tower grows in summer
scienceFacts.description: Heat causes the iron structure to expand, making the tower up to 15 cm taller during hot weather.

scienceFacts.title: Your stomach gets a new lining every few days
scienceFacts.description: Cells lining the stomach are replaced roughly every 3 to 5 days to avoid being dissolved by digestive acid.

scienceFacts.title: Lightning is five times hotter than the Sun's surface
scienceFacts.description: A bolt of lightning can reach around 30,000 K, while the Sun's surface hovers near 5,800 K.

historicalEvents.title: The shortest war in history lasted 38 minutes
historicalEvents.description: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 ended in under 40 minutes after British warships shelled the Sultan's palace.

historicalEvents.title: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the Pyramids
historicalEvents.description: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BCE. Cleopatra lived around 30 BCE. The Moon landing was in 1969, only about 2,000 years after her.

historicalEvents.title: Oxford is older than the Aztec Empire
historicalEvents.description: Teaching existed at Oxford as early as 1096. The Aztec Empire wasn't founded until 1345.

historicalEvents.title: Rome had a population of 1 million in 100 CE
historicalEvents.description: Ancient Rome was one of the first cities to hit a million residents. London wouldn't reach that number again until the 1800s.

historicalEvents.title: Napoleon was once attacked by rabbits
historicalEvents.description: During a hunt in 1807, hundreds of rabbits released for sport instead swarmed Napoleon and his men, forcing them to retreat.

historicalEvents.title: The Great Wall of China took over 2,000 years to build
historicalEvents.description: Construction spanned multiple dynasties from the 7th century BCE to the Ming Dynasty in the 17th century.

historicalEvents.title: The first computer programmer was a woman
historicalEvents.description: Ada Lovelace wrote the first algorithm intended for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine in the 1840s.

historicalEvents.title: The Ottoman Empire lasted 600 years
historicalEvents.description: Founded in 1299 and dissolved in 1922, it was one of the longest-lasting empires in history.

productivityTips.title: Use the two-minute rule
productivityTips.description: If a task takes less than two minutes, do it immediately. It clears mental clutter and prevents small tasks from piling up.

productivityTips.title: Time-block your calendar
productivityTips.description: Assign specific hours to specific tasks. It replaces vague to-do lists with concrete commitments and defends deep work.

productivityTips.title: Batch similar tasks
productivityTips.description: Group emails, calls, and admin work into dedicated blocks. Context switching is one of the biggest silent productivity killers.

productivityTips.title: Follow the 90/20 rule
productivityTips.description: Work in 90-minute focused sprints, then take a 20-minute break. It aligns with the body's natural ultradian rhythm.

productivityTips.title: Write tomorrow's top 3 tonight
productivityTips.description: Deciding priorities in advance removes morning friction and makes it easier to start on real work instead of email.

productivityTips.title: Use single-tasking
productivityTips.description: Studies show multitasking can reduce productivity by up to 40%. Focus on one task until it reaches a natural stopping point.

productivityTips.title: Try the Pomodoro Technique
productivityTips.description: Work for 25 minutes, break for 5. After four cycles, take a longer break. It creates urgency and prevents burnout.

productivityTips.title: Adopt a shutdown ritual
productivityTips.description: End each workday with a short review and a plan for tomorrow. It signals your brain to disconnect and rest fully.

programmingConcepts.title: Idempotency
programmingConcepts.description: An operation is idempotent if running it multiple times produces the same result as running it once. Critical for safe retries in distributed systems and APIs.

programmingConcepts.title: Big-O notation
programmingConcepts.description: A way to describe how an algorithm's runtime or memory scales with input size. O(1) is constant, O(n) is linear, O(n^2) is quadratic.

programmingConcepts.title: Referential transparency
programmingConcepts.description: An expression is referentially transparent if it can be replaced with its value without changing program behavior. It's a foundation of functional programming.

programmingConcepts.title: CAP theorem
programmingConcepts.description: In a distributed data store you can only guarantee two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance. Real systems trade these off constantly.

programmingConcepts.title: Debouncing vs throttling
programmingConcepts.description: Debounce waits for activity to stop before firing. Throttle limits fires to once per interval. Both tame noisy events like scroll or input.

programmingConcepts.title: Pure functions
programmingConcepts.description: A pure function returns the same output for the same input and has no side effects. They're easier to test, cache, and reason about.

programmingConcepts.title: Race conditions
programmingConcepts.description: A bug where the outcome depends on the unpredictable ordering of concurrent operations. Often fixed with locks, atomics, or careful state design.

programmingConcepts.title: Memoization
programmingConcepts.description: Caching the result of an expensive function call so repeated calls with the same arguments return instantly.
